paras: The attempted lynching of Albert Hoyt took place at Astoria, Oregon, on the night of July 7, 1881, when a large crowd gathered at the town jail with a rope prepared to hang Hoyt, a longshoreman accused of raping a nine-year-old girl. The police chief refused to bring the prisoner out and guarded the jail, and Hoyt was later sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary. Pacific Coast papers carried the case as a crime story in which a lynching was narrowly avoided.

Hoyt, described as a married man, was accused of raping Addie Cook, aged nine, the daughter of an actress in Hill's Varieties, on the evening of July 7. According to the Astoria dispatch, the mother discovered what had happened late that night, the child named Hoyt, and the police arrested him shortly afterward. No report gives the race of Hoyt or of the child.

Late that night a large crowd assembled around the jail, and a rope was prepared for a hanging. Chief Barry was asked to take the prisoner to the child for identification and told that she was dying, but, "suspecting their design," he refused and set a guard on the jail. No one was hurt.

The next day Hoyt was examined in the Justice's Court, where the child's stepfather, Cook, appeared armed with a revolver after saying he meant to shoot the prisoner; he was watched and disarmed. Hoyt pleaded guilty, was bound over in $5,000 and was hurried back to prison "to avoid lynching, of which there is great danger," in the words of the shorter wire.

Hoyt was tried in the week before August 18 before Judge Stott in Clatsop County and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary. A Portland dispatch of August 15 reported that Hoyt, already under that sentence, and another prisoner had cut through the floor of the city jail in a failed attempt to escape. No report of arrests or charges against anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.

The fullest account, an Astoria dispatch in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union of July 9, called Hoyt "the villain" and the act an "atrocity," said such outrages were "getting too common" and forecast that Hoyt was "very likely yet to be summarily dealt with by Judge Lynch." A shorter version of the wire, without the jail crowd or the rope, ran on July 10 in the Eureka Daily Sentinel under the headline "Great Danger of His Being Lynched" and in the Daily Los Angeles Herald as "A Disgusting Case of Rape."

In August the Vancouver Independent and the Record-Union reported the sentence in single sentences, the Independent noting that Hoyt had "so narrowly escaped lynching." Those later items named the child Ida Cooke or Ida Cook rather than Addie Cook.

The same court report carries an Astoria dateline of July 8 in the Record-Union and the Los Angeles Herald but July 9 in the Eureka paper, which places the hearing "this morning" rather than "this afternoon."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Hoyt
bases: A crowd gathered at the Astoria jail with a rope prepared to hang a prisoner accused of rape and tried to have him brought out, but the police chief refused and guarded the jail (A1); later reports said he 'narrowly escaped lynching' (A6).
No one was killed: Hoyt was kept in jail, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years (A1, A6, A7). The episode is an attempted lynching by a 'large crowd' acting on a rape accusation (A1).

The Astoria wire (A1, A3, A4) and a separate Vancouver item (A6) agree that Hoyt was in danger of or narrowly escaped lynching, though the jail crowd and rope appear only in the fullest wire text (A1).

accounts.label: Astoria wire, full text
accounts.gist: A large crowd with a rope gathered at the jail late at night and tried to have Hoyt brought out on a pretext; the chief refused and guarded the jail; the dispatch expected Hoyt might still be lynched.

accounts.label: Astoria wire, short text
accounts.gist: Covers only the court hearing: the armed stepfather was disarmed and Hoyt was hurried back to prison to avoid a lynching of which there was 'great danger'.

accounts.label: Vancouver Independent
accounts.gist: Reported his trial and 20-year sentence, saying he had 'so narrowly escaped lynching'.

framing.detail: The fullest wire text treated the guilt as settled ('the villain', 'the criminal'), said such 'outrages' were 'getting too common' and forecast 'Judge Lynch', while reporting the chief's refusal without comment.
Eureka and Los Angeles ran the shorter wire under headlines stressing the charge ('A Disgusting Case of Rape') and the 'Great Danger of His Being Lynched'.
The August follow-ups reported the sentence and a failed jail break in single sentences.

conflicts.note: The July wire and the August follow-ups give different first names.
The same wire text carries different datelines; the Record-Union's July 9 brief says the arrest was 'yesterday' (A2), which fits July 8 for the dispatch.

info: The alleged rape took place on the evening of July 7, 1881, and the crowd gathered at the jail late that night; Hoyt was examined in court on July 8 (Record-Union dateline) or July 9 (Eureka dateline).
Albert Hoyt, a longshoreman and married man, the target of the crowd; no one was killed or injured. His race is not stated.
Accused of raping Addie Cook (later called Ida Cooke or Ida Cook), aged 9, daughter of an actress in Hill's Varieties.
A 'large crowd' at the jail, unnamed; separately the child's stepfather, Cook, came armed to the Police Court and had said he meant to shoot Hoyt.
Sentenced to 20 years in the penitentiary; before transfer he and another prisoner failed in an attempt to break out of the city jail on Aug. 15.
